power.title: Power Analysis Check

table.text: Ideally, we use the fastest evidence accumulating E-process, as it will provide us with the earliest option to stop data collection and potentially maximise resource conservation. We use this optimisation principle to select E-processes in Section 2.1 below. Section 2.3 focuses on how n plan in Protocol 1.1 can be chosen based on a power analysis. As with a classical power analysis, we assume to be given a desired power requirement, e.g. power = 80%, and an expected, or minimum clinically relevant, effect size δ min . Such a δ min is intuitively meaningful when we are not interested in tiny effects of (relatively) costly new treatments; for the case that we are, see Section 3.5. In two-sided settings we refer to data-governing effect sizes δ with |δ| ≥ δ min > 0 as clinically relevant.
table.header: 2 Power and the fastest evidence accumulating E-process under alternatives

table.text: For this reason we developed routines in the safestats package that efficiently sample the first-passage time distribution. Specifically, using (essentially) just Line 3 of R Code 2.1, we simulate (by default) m = 1000 e-value sequences under P δ min, all in under 2.4 seconds on a 2021 iMac M1. 14 Line 4 plots the first-passage time distribution as in 1 library ( safestats ) 2 3 designObj ← designSaviT ( deltaMin =0.5, beta =0.2, testType = " twoSample " ) 4 plot ( designObj ) The top panel of Fig. 7 illustrates the distinct roles of α, δ min, and the desired power for this power analysis. Firstly, α defines the minimum level of evidence for persuasive support, e.g. 1/α = 20, which is shown as the horizontal black line. Secondly, δ min defines the optimal mom E-process which is expressed by the steepness of the average upward drift of the e-value sequences. Lastly, the blue histogram shows that after n1 = n2 = 100 observations, a wee few more than 800 out of the m = 1000 e-value sequences correctly resulted in a first option to stop in favour of the presence of a treatment effect. Hence, by monitoring e n ≥ 1/α up to n plan = 100 we are able to detect a true treatment effect size of δ min with at least 80% power. To acknowledge that n plan is derived from simulations, the design object (Fig. 8) also reports twice the bootstrap standard error of 5.69. It also shows an average sample size of n mean = 59 for both groups, which is the average between the first times N < n plan at which e N ≥ 1/α occurs, and N = n plan for those e-value sequences (green) that continued until n plan . In comparison, a classical p < 0.05 test with the same α, power, δ min always requires n1 = n2 = 64. Hence, under P δ min, the mom savi t-test will require on average 5 fewer (but in the worst-case, 36 more) participants in both groups compared to the classical p < 0.05 test. The flexibility of e-value based tests comes at the price of a larger sample size to plan for, but Fig. 7 shows that in return there is about 59% probability to realise a stopped experiment before n = 64, whenever δ = δ min.

table.text: A reasonable estimate of the underlying standardised effect size based on the original findings (Gray & Wegner, 2009, Study 1a) is within (0.769, 0.872). 19 We err on the side of caution by using the lower bound for our power analysis. Furthermore, we can argue for a one-sided test (Grünwald & Koolen, 2025), as the working hypothesis deals with the offending adult man being perceived as more, not less, responsible compared to the offending baby. A classical power analysis shows that for δ min = 0.769 and power = 80%, the one-sided p-value test should be performed after gathering data from n1 = n2 = 22 participants in each group.

There were 57 Many Labs 2 replication attempts that fulfilled the inclusion criteria, of which 3 (5.26%) yielded a significant p-value less than α = 0.05. These conclusions were based on n1 = 3439 and n2 = 3508 participants. 22 A reasonable estimate of the datagoverning standardised effect size based on the original findings in Zhong and Liljenquist (2006, Study 2) is within (0.909, 1.429). As before, we err on the side of caution by using the lower bound for our design. A classical power analysis shows that for δ min = 0.909 and power = 80% power, the one-sided p < α test should be conducted after gathering data from n1 = n2 = 16 participants in each group. Lines 2 to 3 of R Code 4.1 with deltaMin <-(4.95-3.75)/1.32 show that with the correspondingly tuned mom E-process, we should plan for n plan = n1 = n2 = 27 participants in each group to observe e n ≥ 20 with 80% power under δ min = 0.909. If δ = δ min the procedure is expected to stop after testing n mean = 17 participants in each group. 23 For most replication attempts the one-sided e-value test hit 22 Unfortunately, we were unable to retrieve the correct "bogota" data from the data sets uploaded at https://osf.io/8cd4r/, which is why our results differ slightly compared to what is reported in Klein et al. (2018). 23 For a two-sided e-value test we require n plan = 33 and the procedure stops after nmean = 21 in each group n plan . We acquired e n ≥ 1/α = 20 in one out of a total of 57 replication attempts (1.75%) based on a total of n1 = 1427 and n2 = 1441 participants per group, thus, n1 = 25.04 and n2 = 25.28 on average. If the magnitude of the data governing δ was indeed at least δ min, then we have provided such δ ample chance to yield persuasive evidence. Since this did not occur for most replication attempts, we infer that the postulate δ ≥ δ min is unlikely with high probability. Moreover, we come to this conclusion with 2012 and 2067 fewer participants per group, which is a reduction of 58.5% and 58.9% from the total sample sizes used in the original analysis. We would like to reiterate the point that with e-values we do not have to stop at the first-passage time e n ≥ 1/α, nor at n plan . Due to E-processes being robust to any stopping time, there is no need to discard newly available data once the test is conducted or the confidence interval is computed, as is the case with a classical analysis.

There are circumstances where no minimal clinical relevant effect size δ min can be specified. Nonetheless, it is still possible to choose a tuning parameter and conduct a savi ttest. For instance, in a practical scenarios where the available budget forms the bottleneck of our investigation, yielding a restriction on the sample sizes, say, at most n1 = n2 = 40. Before running Protocol 1.1 with n plan = 40, we might want to get an indication of the δ that we can detect with, say, 80% power. Providing the designSaviT function with α, n plan, power, e.g. Lines 3 and 4 of R Code 2.1, reveals that the smallest effect that we can detect with 80% probability is about δ min = 0.882.

Subject experts might claim that an effect size of δ = 0.7 is more realistic. Such an effect can still be detected if we sample up to n1 = n2 = 40, but with smaller probability. Providing designSaviT with α, n plan, δ min, e.g. Lines 5 and 6 of R Code 2.1, we can conclude that under P δ with δ = 0.7 we have 64.2 % power to observe e n ≥ 20 by monitoring up to n plan = 40.
table.statistical_test_other: Power analysis for detecting effect size δ = 0.7 with sample sizes n1 = n2 = 40 and significance level α (implied)

table.text: The fact that the grow E-process yields the lowest n plan is due to it being the fastest evidence accumulating procedure amongst all E-processes. However, in case the grow t-test was optimised for δ min = 0.5, but the data-governing effect size is actually δ = 0.2, then the grow E-process requires many more samples to yield e n ≥ 1/α with 80% power. If the grow E-process were tuned to δmin = 0.2 from the beginning, then it only needs n plan = 531 instead of n plan = 2612, which equates to a relative increase of 392%. The relative increase is much less for mom (36.6%), eGauss (9.2%), and eCauchy (8.0%), though, the latter two types have higher baselines (643 and 686 compared to 596 respectively), see also Fig. 9.

Upon reaching n plan without the e-value sequence crossing 1/α, we can halt data collection, maintain the null hypothesis as the status quo, and assert that the effect is not clinically relevant, with a type II error rate of at most 1 -power. Alternatively, we can also continue sampling if the e-value looks promising and we are keen to investigate a smaller effect. Similar conclusions can be reached by exploring the anytime-valid confidence intervals. The role of the planned sample size is to guarantee at least, e.g. power = 80% probability to gain persuasive support for a treatment effect under continuous monitoring. R Code 2.2: The design function designSaviT() takes as input α and any two of the three quantities power, δ min, n plan to yield an indication of the remaining quantity, and the optimal parameter as output. Lines 1 and 2 specify as input power, δ min and outputs n plan, Lines 3 and 4 take as input power, n plan and outputs an indication of δ min, Lines 5 and 6 take as input δ min, n plan and yield power, thus, expected power. Lines 7 and 8 take as input n plan and yield the parameter such that at n plan the confidence interval is the narrowest.

We recommend the mom E-process (Johnson & Rossell, 2010) as a default procedure, because the resulting savi t-test provides the best balance between efficiency and robustness to the choice of δ min, as a result of specifying a continuous prior as opposed to point priors (e.g. grow in purple in Fig. 4). It also yields well-concentrated anytime-valid confidence intervals (blue curves in Fig. 10). Table 2 shows n plan for various types of E-processes when α = 0.05 and power = 80% in the two-sample t-test setting with n = n1 = n 2 for δ min = 0.5 and δ min = 0.2. The ordering of the E-process types in terms of the lowest n plan remains the same for various values of α, power, δ min, e.g. Fig. 9. For a fair comparison between the four types of E-processes, we chose the fastest evidence accumulating E-process for each type (e.g. Section 1.3.5). The third and last columns also show the average sample sizes. For instance, under δ = δ min = 0.5, the first two rows show that the procedure, which monitors the grow (or mom) e-value up to n plan and stops as soon as e n ≥ 1/α, will, on average, stop after n mean = n1 = n2 = 56 (or n1 = n2 = 59) participants. ::: {.callout-tip title="Learn More" collapse="true"}

Power analyses need to contain the following information to be interpretable: the type of power analysis, the statistical test, the software used, sample size, critical alpha criterion, power level, effect size, and an effect size metric. In addition, it is recommended to make sure the power analysis is reproducible (by sharing the code, or a screenshot, of the power analysis), and to provide good arguments for why the study was designed to detect an effect of this size.

For an a-priori power analysis, where the sample size is determined, reporting all information would look like:

> An a priori power analysis for an independent samples t-test, conducted using the pwr.t.test function from pwr (Champely, 2020), indicated that for a Cohen's d = 0.5, an alpha level of 0.05, and a desired power level of 80% required at least 64 participants in each group.

For a sensitivity power analysis, this sentence would look like:

> A sensitivity power analysis for an independent samples t-test, conducted using the pwr.t.test function from pwr (Champely, 2020), indicated that with 64 participants in each group, and an alpha level of 0.05, a desired power level of 80% was reached for an effect size of d = 0.5.

report: Reporting *p* values imprecisely (e.g., *p* < .05) reduces transparency, reproducibility, and re-use (e.g., in *p* value meta-analyses). Best practice is to report exact p-values with three decimal places (e.g., *p* = .032) unless *p* values are smaller than 0.001, in which case you can use *p* < .001.

This module sometimes flags false positives when sentences discuss how p-value thresholds were set. It can also miss an imprecise p-value that is reported against a threshold (e.g., "decreased at the *p* < .05 significance threshold").

#### Code Comments
Best programming practice is to add comments to code, to explain what the code does (to yourself in the future, or peers who want to re-use your code). All your code files had comments.
#### Missing Files
All files loaded in the code were present in the repository.
#### Absolute Paths

Best programming practice is to use relative file paths (e.g., './files') instead of absolute file paths (e.g., 'C://Lakens/project_dir/files') as these folder names do not exist on other computers. No absolute file paths were found in any of the code files.
#### Working Directory (setwd)

Best programming practice is to avoid `setwd()` in analysis code: it hardcodes an assumption about the working directory (often an absolute path on the author's own machine), so the code breaks when run anywhere else. Keep the working directory as the caller sets it and use relative paths. No `setwd()` calls were found in any of the code files.
#### Package Installation (install.packages)

Best programming practice is to avoid `install.packages()` in analysis code: it installs software on whoever runs the script without asking, which is at minimum disruptive (an unexpected install, network access, a package version the author never tested against) and at worst a security risk if it points at an untrusted repository. Document required packages instead (a README, or a list of them: an `renv.lock`/`DESCRIPTION` for R, a `requirements.txt` for Python). `install.packages()` calls were found in 3 code files.

This module runs automated data-quality checks (empty columns, SPSS filter variables, category casing, stray whitespace, numbers stored as text, problematic and colliding column names, mixed text encodings, personal information, spreadsheet formatting, and careless responding) on the extracted data files.
We examined 54 columns across 4 data files.
#### Issues Identified

8 file/column combinations have at least one issue.

**About the personal-information flags.** These are pattern matches, not confirmed disclosures, and they are tuned to over-report rather than miss something. Expect false positives:

- **Column names** are matched against identifying words in English and other European languages (`email`, `telefoonnummer`, `geboortedatum`, ...). A column called `phone_number` flags whether or not it holds one, and an empty or already-anonymised column flags on its name alone.
- **Values** are matched against the shape of an identifier. An IP address pattern also matches a version string or a dotted numeric code; a card-number pattern requires both a real issuer prefix and a checksum, but a long numeric ID can still coincide.
- **Free text** is flagged when a column holds long, mostly-distinct prose — the shape open-ended answers take. Most such columns contain no names at all.

A flag means *look at this column*. Where the data is already de-identified (an `ip` column reading `Anonymized`, a `name` column the authors emptied), no action is needed.

```{r} #| echo: false # table data -------------------------------------- table <- structure(list(File = c("grayData.RData", "safestats_0.8.8.tar.gz/safestats/build/vignette.rds", "safestats_0.8.8.tar.gz/safestats/build/vignette.rds", "safestats_0.8.8.tar.gz/safestats/build/vignette.rds", "v2/grayData.RData", "v2/safestats_0.8.8.tar.gz/safestats/build/vignette.rds", "v2/safestats_0.8.8.tar.gz/safestats/build/vignette.rds", "v2/safestats_0.8.8.tar.gz/safestats/build/vignette.rds" ), Column = c("Execution", "Depends", "Keywords", "Title", "Execution", "Depends", "Keywords", "Title"), Issues = c("⬜ Empty column — Column is empty: all 8042 values are missing", "⬜ Empty column — Column is empty: all 9 values are missing", "⬜ Empty column — Column is empty: all 9 values are missing", "🔒 Personally Identifying Information — Free-text column (median 70 characters, 100% distinct, 22% written ...", "⬜ Empty column — Column is empty: all 8042 values are missing", "⬜ Empty column — Column is empty: all 9 values are missing", "⬜ Empty column — Column is empty: all 9 values are missing", "🔒 Personally Identifying Information — Free-text column (median 70 characters, 100% distinct, 22% written ..." )), row.names = c(NA, -8L), class = "data.frame") # display table ----------------------------------- metacheck::report_table(table, "auto", 20, FALSE) ```
#### Careless Responding
No file could be screened for careless responding.

**What this does not cover.** Only 0 of 4 data files could be screened: the rest had no detectable multi-item scale block, or too few respondents. Even in a screened file, these checks only look at multi-item rating scales — the only place where a repeated or flat answer pattern is interpretable. Single questions, open text, demographics and any item outside a detected scale block are never examined. A respondent can therefore answer most of a survey carelessly and still not be flagged here, and finding nothing is not evidence that a dataset is free of careless responding.

#### File paths

Every data path in the code works in the repository as deposited. The code reads files that are only inside `safestats_0.8.8.tar.gz`, `v2/safestats_0.8.8.tar.gz`, and no script unpacks them. We unpacked them in their folder before the run. So that others can run the code as deposited, start the code with a line that unpacks them (such as `unzip("safestats_0.8.8.tar.gz")` in R), or upload the files unpacked.
#### Execution

**The code was run.** Each script ran in an isolated Docker container against a throwaway copy of the repository, in the run order above, with a 300-second per-script timeout. Of 14 scripts: 1 ran without error, 10 errored, 0 timed out, 3 could not run because one of its own dependencies is unavailable, 0 did not parse. Running against current package versions: a break can reflect version drift, which argues for pinning versions.

info.title: Safe Anytime-Valid Inference: Practical Maximally Flexible Sampling Designs for Experiments Based on e-Values

text.text: We demonstrate how e-values simplify both experimental design and the inference process.
With e-values researchers can perform anytime-valid tests and construct confidence intervals that maintain type I error control regardless of the sample size.
This enables real-time monitoring of evidence as data are collected, permitting early termination of experiments without intolerably inflating the risk of false discoveries.
Early stopping not only conserves resources, but also mitigates risk for participants in clinical settings.

Anytime-valid tests allow for optional continuation, that is, the extension of an experiment, for instance if more funds become available, or even if the evidence looks promising and the funding agency, a reviewer, or an editor urges the experimenter to collect more data.

Analogously, a researcher can be assured that a 95% anytime-valid confidence interval will, with at least 95% probability, cover the true effect size regardless of how, or even if, data collection is stopped.
We use the free and open-source software package safestats implemented in R to illustrate the practical benefits of this novel inference framework.

text.formatted: working hypothesis appear "significant", even when it truly is not. <ref type="bibr">Simmons, Nelson, and Simonsohn (2011, p. 4</ref>) therefore emphasised the need for transparency and adherence to these sampling rules, urging reviewers to enforce compliance.

text.text: But this solution ultimately relies on eliminating flexibility by confining researchers to a rigid sampling protocol, all in service of an old-fashioned statistical inference tool developed back in the 1930s.
In practice, however, even the most carefully planned studies face setbacks such as slow recruitment, budget shortfalls, or unforeseen crises like pandemics.
Being left with invalid inferences after managing such challenges can be both discouraging and counterproductive.
Instead of tying researchers to rigid classical tools that demand strict sampling plans, we introduce anytime-valid tests and e-value based confidence intervals.
These methods allow researchers to dynamically decide whether to continue or stop an experiment, all without breaking statistical guarantees.
Reviewers benefit too, since they no longer need to verify adherence to rigid sampling protocols.

Our primary contribution lies in offering insightful yet non-binding recommendations for maximally flexible sample sizes, providing clear guidance on how to allocate resources efficiently when designing and conducting experiments.

In a nutshell (all jargon will be explained further below), we provide planned sample sizes n plan at which a desired power at a guessed (or minimally clinically relevant) effect size is guaranteed; non-binding means that both the e-value based tests and confidence intervals remain valid irrespective of whether the planned sample size is actually realised, or whether the guessed effect size is even approximately correctwe may always stop early or sample new data points at will.
These planned sample sizes can easily be obtained with the safestats R software package as elaborated on in Section 2.3.
Before doing so, we first address the challenges of monitoring a p < α test in Section 1.2 and demonstrate how e-values resolve these issues in Section 1.3.
text.formatted: Before doing so, we first address the challenges of monitoring a p < α test in Section 1.2 and demonstrate how e-values resolve these issues in Section 1.3.

text.text: More generally: • Section 1 focuses on type I errors, specifically addressing scenarios where a true treatment effect is absent.
This section is more detailed, as it establishes the notation and provides the main motivation for e-values.
• Section 2 shifts the focus to power and investigates the behaviour of e-values under alternatives (when an effect is truly present).
• Section 3 provides practical recommendations on the choice of e-value procedures in the t-test setting.
• Section 4 demonstrates how a planned e-value analysis enables reliable conclusions using approximately 58% and 70% fewer data points in two real-world examples.

• Before digging into details, the hurried reader may want to consult the concluding Section 5 which summarises advantages but also lists potential disadvantages of using e-value based inference methods, as well as further important (mostly advantageous) aspects of e-values that we could not cover here in detail.
This introduction to e-values is intended for practitioners who wish to make reliable inferences with minimal statistical hurdles.

It focuses on accessibility for an applied audience, leaving rigorous mathematical treatment to specialised works such as those by Grünwald, De Heide, and Koolen (2024), Howard, Ramdas, McAuliffe, and Sekhon (2021), Ramdas, Grünwald, Vovk, and Shafer (2023), and Shafer (2021).

text.text: The number of such applications is growing rapidly, which makes this small sample somewhat arbitrary.
To make the exposition concrete, we consider two classical testing scenarios: first, a simplistic one, in which we get to see independent tosses of a coin, and aim to test whether the coin is fair.
This example will only be used in Section 1.1 to harness intuition.
The second scenario is more practically relevant, and used in all subsequent sections: the standard experimental setup where two groups, say, treatment and control, are being compared.
As usual, individuals in each group are assumed to have normally distributed responses with unknown population means µ 1 , µ 2 , respectively, and unknown population standard deviation σ.
To argue for the effectiveness of the treatment, we test the null hypothesis that states H 0 ∶ φ ∶= µ 1 -µ2 = φ 0 , where φ 0 is a postulated (known) null value, typically, φ0 = 0.
Under the null hypothesis, any discrepancy between the postulated null value φ 0 and the observed sample mean difference x1 -x2 is solely attributable to random variation.
The conventional approach uses a two-sample t-test, conducted at a pre-registered -thus, data-blind -sample size or "time point" n.
At n, data collection stops, the test is conducted, and a decision is made to either reject, if p < α, or to not reject the null hypothesis, if p ≥ α.
text.formatted: At n, data collection stops, the test is conducted, and a decision is made to either reject, if p < α, or to not reject the null hypothesis, if p ≥ α.

text.text: As usual, α represents the tolerable type I error, the probability (i.e. relative frequency) with which a testing procedure is allowed to produce a false null rejection.

To ease exposition, we think of time n as the sample size(s) and assume that n = n1 = n 2. 1 Determining n at which data collection has to stop and the p < α test is conducted is challenging: if the sample size is set too low, we risk losing statistical power, therefore, missing a true treatment effect with too high probability; conversely, setting n too high wastes valuable resources.
text.formatted: To ease exposition, we think of time n as the sample size(s) and assume that n = n1 = n 2. <ref type="foot" target="#foot_0">1</ref> Determining n at which data collection has to stop and the p < α test is conducted is challenging: if the sample size is set too low, we risk losing statistical power, therefore, missing a true treatment effect with too high probability; conversely, setting n too high wastes valuable resources.

text.text: To circumvent this problem, we propose dynamically determining the sample sizes by tracking a sequence of e-values, where e stands for the evidence against the null hypothesis indicated by the accumulating data.
An e-value of 0 means no evidence, 1 means neutral evidence, and values above 1 indicate evidence against the null.
The larger the e-value, the stronger the evidence, which in principle can grow without bound, representing irrefutable evidence against the null.

As data accumulate, we observe a sequence of e-values written as e ∶= (e 1 , e 2 , . . . , e n , . . . , e n plan ), where n plan is some time horizon (not a fixed sample size), which we arbitrarily set to n plan = 200 for the moment.
At each time point n the e-value e n is a non-negative number forming, for example, the sequence e = (1, 0.83, . . . , 27).
As soon as e n passes 1/α, we can reliably stop an experiment in favour of a treatment effect.
Importantly, when there truly is no effect, there is at most α (e.g. α = 0.05) probability that we will ever observe misleading evidence against the null hypothesis larger than 1/α = 20.
This result is known as Ville's inequality, which we use to motivate the formal definition of e-values and E-processes in Section 1.3.3 below.
In this section we connect e-values to more established perspectives of inference.
Each paragraph is tailored to a specific mode of inference, which can be safely skipped by a reader who is unfamiliar with the corresponding perspective.
To make the connections, we consider a null hypothesis that specifies a single data-generating distribution.
For instance, in the coin flipping problem where we are interested in testing whether the coin is fair.
The coin flips are denoted by (X 1 , X 2 , . . .), and at each flip i the outcome is either 1, if the coin lands heads and 0 otherwise.
The coin is fair if θ = 1/2, where θ is the probability of the random variable X i having outcome 1.
Readers familiar with likelihood ratios might feel assured that any likelihood ratio with the null distribution in the denominator constitutes an E-process, a procedure that outputs e-values.
For instance, the likelihood ratio that in the numerator fixes an alternative probability θ ≠ 1/2.
The E-variable at the nth flip then depends on y representing the number of 1s observed in X 1 , . . . , X n :
Appendix D shows more generally that any likelihood ratio with density p(x n ) in the denominator forms an E-process of the simple null P , such as p(x n ) = (1/2) n in Eq. ( 1).

As discussed in Box 1, 3 such a likelihood ratio process can be given a very concrete betting interpretation.
This interpretation extends to cases where there is no likelihood function, and provides heuristics for what is and what is not allowed with e-values (Section 1.4).
Readers familiar with Bayes factor testing might find solace in the fact that we can take any prior π(θ) and use q(x n ) ∶= ∫ f (x n | θ)π(θ)dθ in the numerator of the likelihood ratio.
Hence, when the null is simple, the Bayes factor is an E-variable.

Readers familiar with classical Neyman-Pearson testing theory may be aware that, for simple alternative and null hypotheses, the most powerful p < α test of level α -at a fixed sample size n-is equivalent to an e q n ≥ c n,α test that rejects the null if the likelihood ratio exceeds a threshold that depends on both α and n.

We may always interpret an E-process as a bettor's potential wealth in an ongoing multi-round game, in which no money is expected to be gained if the null hypothesis holds true.
We explain the precise rules of the game in the simplest setting, where the E-process takes the form of a likelihood ratio process.
In this setting the bettor starts with initial capital e1 = 1, say, dollar, and the pay-off per round is given by o(x), where x is an outcome taking values in a finite set, say, {red, black}.
If the null hypothesis corresponds to p(red) = p(black) = 1/2, as for a roulette table without the green 0 outcome, then the game maker (i.e. the casino/nature) can set o(x) = 1/p(x) = 2.

At each round n, before seeing the outcome of X n , the bettor determines a strategy for allocating her current wealth e n-1 across all possible outcomes; for example, q(red ) × e1 = 4/3; the money put on black is lost.
Thus, at round n, after observing x n , the bettor's accumulated wealth becomes
For example, after observing a sequence (red, red, black) the bettor above would have accumulated (4/3) 2 (2/3) = 1.19 dollar.

If (as in the example above, with the null a 'real casino') the o(x) is set such that the bettor is not expected to gain money if the null hypothesis is true, then (and only then) is the potential wealth process E = (E 1 , E 2 , . . .) an E-process of P .
It further is a good E-process if the bettor is expected to get rich fast when the alternative is true.
Betting with strategy q(red) = 2/3 at round n makes sense if, based on data so far, the bettor thinks that there is a substantially larger probability of observing red compared to black.
If this is really the case, then the bettor's wealth E n will grow exponentially fast.
The higher this wealth, the more evidence is acquired against the null.

By refining the game, the betting analogy can be extended to composite nulls and continuous outcomes as is the case for the T -statistic: every E-process has a sequential betting interpretation, which can be used to gain intuition.

For instance, the fact that E-processes preserve type I error control under optional stopping is the same mathematical phenomenon as the fact that there is at most 1/c probability of you multiplying your initial capital in a real casino by a factor c -no matter what betting strategy you use or what rule is used to stop betting.

The fact that a legitimate stopping time (Section 1.3) may depend on past data but not on the future corresponds to the truism that your decision to stop betting in a real casino may depend on what you have seen so far but not on what you will see in the future.

text.text: The crucial difference lies in the protocol.
For its type I error guarantee and power, the SPRT must follow a fixed rule: stop and reject as soon as e n ≥ (1 -β)/α, or stop and accept the null the first time e n ≤ (1 -α)/β.
With ebased testing, by contrast, the type I error guarantee holds under arbitrary, even unknown, stopping rules; see Section 1.3.1 for further discussion.

For arbitrary composite null hypotheses, as in the common two-sample t-test, the connection between E-processes and Bayes factors, likelihood ratios, and p-values becomes considerably intricate: Neither the generalised likelihood ratio nor the Bayes factor is then automatically an E-process (e.g.
Appendix I).
Both the evidential interpretation of the e-value and the anytime-valid rejection rule e ≥ 1/α nevertheless carry over.

Moreover, E-processes may be constructed in very general, nonparametric settings where they look very different from (generalised) likelihood ratios, and Bayes factors (Chugg, Ramdas, & Grünwald, 2026).

text.text: Any deviation in the sampling plan invalidates this interpretation, which then leads to wrong conclusions.
The desire for a measure of evidence that is resilient to sampling to a foregone conclusion can be seen as the main motivation for e-values.
Its definition rests on one key requirement: controlling the risk of false evidence -that is, bounding the probability of observing misleadingly large evidence against a true null hypothesis.
Meeting this requirement depends on two technical concepts.
The first is stopping times, which models when data collection ends, whether by design or external factors.
The second is Markov's inequality, a technique that uses the expected value to bound the probability of extreme outcomes.
Together, they provide the backbone for the robustness we want, as we explained below.
In brief, we view a sequence of e-values as an outcome of a random process E ∶= (E 1 , E 2 , . . . , E n , . . .).
This process is designed so that, at any stopping time, its expected value never exceeds one.
We denote by E n the anticipated evidence at time n, written in uppercase to emphasise its dependence on not yet seen data.
Once the data at time n are observed, the random variable E n takes on a value (e.g. e n = 7) and loses its randomness.
Hence, a random process E formalises the sequential procedure that converts accumulating data into a running sequence of e-values that evolves over time.
We next elaborate on the practical relevance of stopping times through examples, then show how knowledge of a random process's expectation yields the desired control.
A stopping time N at which data collection will be halted is determined by a decision rule that at most uses the data observed up to that point (i.e.
N may not depend on data observed after time N ).
Here are two (familiar) examples: (a) The deterministic stopping rule to terminate data collection at a fixed time, say, N = 200, after observing n1 = n2 = 200 pairs, is a stopping time.
Halting is not influenced by any observation, particularly those after N = 200.
(b) Stopping at first-passage time N , the first point when e N ≥ 1/α or p N < α, uses only the data collected up to time N.

text.text: Adapting stopping rules (a) and (b) to the available data yields legitimate stopping times: (c) Delayed first-passage time: Assume that the first-passage time N occurs early on.
To increase our confidence in the finding, we require the e-value to remain above 1/α = 20 for, say, an additional 6 time points before actually stopping.
(d) Forced continuation: We observed e = 12, but a reviewer, convinced that the effect is real, insists that we collect another 37 observations before we conclude the experiment.
Stopping after these additional 37 observations is a stopping time.
(e) Optimistic continuation: A statistician tells us to stop data collection for the null the first instance e N ≤ 0.21, and to stop for a treatment effect as soon as e N ≥ 16.
During data acquisition e n ≤ 0.21 is observed, but the optimistic principle investigator entices us to continue sampling until e N ≥ 16.
The first time N at which e N ≥ 16 occurs after first observing e n ≤ 0.21 is a stopping time.
Note that the last two stopping times incorporate hopeful intentions.

Sometimes we are forced to stop due to external causes, which are also examples of stopping times: (f) The resource-exhausting stopping time is the moment when data collection is halted due to depleted funds, a malfunctioning measurement instrument such as an fMRI scanner, a catastrophic event, or mandatory shutdowns due to a pandemic.
(g) Frustrated stopping time: The moment the study stops, because the principal investigators quit their jobs in rage due to their constant struggles with a particularly evil printer.

(h) Convenient stopping time: The point in time when a meeting is finally scheduled with a funding agent, governing board and ethics committee, and the data analytic results can finally be reviewed (e.g.
Ter Schure et al., 2022).

More formally, the minimum between two stopping times N and M is also a stopping time.
For instance, N could be the first-passage time E N ≥ 1/α, and M corresponds to some planned sample size n plan derived from a power analysis.
Taking an additional minimum with the time at which resources (e.g. funding, time, or energy) are exhausted yields a model for a stopping time in real-world applications.
Every process eventually stops and we write Ñ for this (potentially unknown in advance) time at which data collection will be halted.

Even though the stopping time Ñ is unknown, we want to base our inference on a random process E that, under the null hypothesis, has only a small probability of producing misleadingly large e-values when stopped.
For this, we employ Markov's inequality (see Appendix B for a proof), which bounds the probability of any non-negative random variable X exceeding c > 0 by 1/c times its expectation.

text.text: We are, however, not limited to choosing a single value, such as δ s = 0.5.
Instead, we can spread our bet by taking a weighted average over the tuning parameter δ s and construct what is known as a mixture E-process with respect to a prior π(δ s ).

The prior is selected before data observation as in Bayesian statistics.

text.text: The crucial condition is that the decision to stop may depend only on the data observed so far -never on data still to come, but also not on data already in hand but selectively set aside.

Suppose a researcher collects n = 100 observations, shuffles them into a new order, notices that the e-value first crosses 1/α after m = 86 of the reshuffled observations, and reports e 86 while discarding the remaining 14.
This is not a legitimate stopping time: the choice to stop at 86 was made with all 100 observations in hand, so it depends on "future" data.
Dropping 14 observations as "outliers" because they lowered the e-value is the same violation in a different guise. 11 A second trap is reporting the running maximum.
text.formatted: Dropping 14 observations as "outliers" because they lowered the e-value is the same violation in a different guise. <ref type="foot" target="#foot_5">11</ref> A second trap is reporting the running maximum.

text.text: Imagine that the sequence e 1 , e 2 , . . . , e 100 peaked at n = 37 and never returned to that height.
Ignoring X 38 , X 39 , . . . , X 100 and reporting the largest seen e 37 overstates the evidence against the null and carries some subtle consequences; see Appendix G for more details.
Before collecting the observation at time n + 1, it is allowed to use the observations up to time n to decide which group to sample from next (Ly, Boehm, & Koolen, 2026).
text.formatted: Before collecting the observation at time n + 1, it is allowed to use the observations up to time n to decide which group to sample from next <ref type="bibr" target="#b34">(Ly, Boehm, & Koolen, 2026)</ref>.

text.text: Validity breaks, however, if the group label is selected after the outcome at time n + 1 is known.
Cherry-picking the E-process from the vast collection E(M 0 ) after seeing the data also undermines the claim that e n ≥ 1/α is rare under the null.
Cheating is still prohibited within this framework of inference, and it is not anticipated to be permitted within any reasonable framework of inference (Steinhilber, Schnuerch, & Schubert, 2025).

text.text: The betting interpretation as described in Box 1 provides a heuristic to establish what remains valid with e-values.
Before seeing the outcome at time n + 1, we are allowed to pick our betting strategy -thus, the mixture π and the savi test defining parametersbased on the information up to time n, but not after.
Similarly, given data at round n, we can choose the roulette table to play on at time n + 1.
After the outcome is revealed on our table, we cannot take our bet back and claim that we played on another table.
Analogously, once we keep on playing and our wealth decreased, then we cannot walk off the table with the highest wealth that we gathered but lost along the way.
The remedy for all of these traps is the same: choose the E-process before data collection begins, and pre-register that choice.
Below, we demonstrate how the safestats software package supports this practice.
Once an E-process is selected, Ville's and Markov's inequality Eq. ( 6) ensure that inference remains safe and anytime-valid.
text.formatted: Once an E-process is selected, Ville's and Markov's inequality Eq. ( <ref type="formula" target="#formula_10">6</ref>) ensure that inference remains safe and anytime-valid.

text.text: This is achieved by bounding the probability of an E-process producing misleading evidence, even under the most aggressive first-passage time rule, which rejects the null as soon as e n ≥ 1/α, while continually extending the time horizon to maximise the potential for misdirection.
Hence, instead of fixing the sample size in advance, we propose to use the datadriven procedure as described in Protocol 1.1 in R code.
The first occurrence of e n ≥ 1/α does not mandate stopping or the rejection of the null hypothesis.
Instead, it serves as the earliest signal to consider halting data collection as a result of persuasive evidence.
Sampling can safely continue, allowing further data to potentially lower the e-value and revisit any preliminary hard conclusions regarding the null hypothesis.
Similarly, we are free to continue sampling even if n plan is reached and more funding came available.
Additional data always enhance inference, for example by tightening the mom type confidence intervals.
In the end, the realised e-value is most naturally understood as a continuous measure of evidence against the null (e.g. Chugg et al., 2026; Koning, 2024).

Ideally, we use the fastest evidence accumulating E-process, as it will provide us with the earliest option to stop data collection and potentially maximise resource conservation.

Such a δ min is intuitively meaningful when we are not interested in tiny effects of (relatively) costly new treatments; for the case that we are, see Section 3.5.

There are circumstances where no minimal clinical relevant effect size δ min can be specified.
Nonetheless, it is still possible to choose a tuning parameter and conduct a savi ttest.
For instance, in a practical scenarios where the available budget forms the bottleneck of our investigation, yielding a restriction on the sample sizes, say, at most n1 = n2 = 40.
Before running Protocol 1.1 with n plan = 40, we might want to get an indication of the δ that we can detect with, say, 80% power.
Providing the designSaviT function with α, n plan , power, e.g.
Lines 3 and 4 of R Code 2.1, reveals that the smallest effect that we can detect with 80% probability is about δ min = 0.882.
Subject experts might claim that an effect size of δ = 0.7 is more realistic.
Such an effect can still be detected if we sample up to n1 = n2 = 40, but with smaller probability.
Providing designSaviT with α, n plan , δ min , e.g.
Lines 5 and 6 of R Code 2.1, we can conclude that under P δ with δ = 0.7 we have 64.2 % power to observe e n ≥ 20 by monitoring up to n plan = 40.

If any of these prospective analyses show that (a) the planned sample size is too high, (b) the smallest detectable effect size is unrealistically large, or (c) the power is too low, then we can either request more funds to invite the derived additional number of participants to the study, or decide, in advance, that it is futile to conduct this experiment, and spend our time and efforts on different endeavours instead.
If neither δ min nor a desired power is known in advance, we can run designSaviT with only α, n plan , e.g.
Lines 7 and 8 of R Code 2.1.

The key point is that prospective power analyses for savi t-tests can be done with just a few lines of code.
The resulting designObj defines the type of E-process to use, the tuning parameter for inference, and the duration over which the null hypothesis should be tested.

To prevent concerns about cherry-picking, this information (such as which type of E-process is chosen for inference) can be saved and submitted to an online pre-registration repository before conducting the experiment.
Importantly, the planned sample sizes are indicative only and do not represent a binding commitment regarding the number of samples to be collected.
The realised sample size at which the experiment can be stopped can be smaller(larger) than planned, when the true effect is larger(smaller) than minimal clinically relevant.
Regardless of the specific value of the data-governing δ, we can safely adapt our experiments to the available evidence, as quantified by the e-value.
In Section 1.3.5 we listed four types of E-processes in the t-test setting.
Each type provides type I error control over time, though some are better suited for certain purposes than others.
In this section, we provide insights that guide the choice of the savi t-test.

It will therefore yield irrefutable evidence against the null in case the data are overwhelmingly informative.

Another reason to choose eCauchy would be its overall robustness to the specification of δ min.

text.text: The situation is then arguably exploratory, whereas the discussion regarding priors and tuning parameters above is concerned with a prospective analysis.
Regardless of the specific method (e.g. grow, mom, eGauss, or eCauchy) and the tuning parameters, all savi t-tests remain reliable, in the sense that they provide type I error guarantees.
Regardless of the tuning parameters, the mom, eGauss, and eCauchy methods put non-zero prior mass on every region in the parameter space.
As a consequence, in addition to providing type I error guarantees, they adapt to the value of the underlying effect size, no matter how small, as data accumulate.
Therefore, if the actual δ ≠ 0 and we keep sampling data, they will eventually reject the null; in other words, for large sample sizes, their power tends to 1.
For instance, we can safely use the mom E-process with tuning parameter g mom = 0.5 2 2 , which is used when no design object is specified.
In particular, while 0.5 is the optimal choice if δ = 0.5, the resulting test will still reject after sufficiently many samples, for any other δ ≠ 0.5, as long as δ > 0.
text.formatted: In particular, while 0.5 is the optimal choice if δ = 0.5, the resulting test will still reject after sufficiently many samples, for any other δ ≠ 0.5, as long as δ > 0.

text.text: The sample size at which we reject under a very small but non-zero δ will tend to be somewhat smaller though for eGauss and eCauchy equipped with the corresponding tuning parameter, simply because they put much larger prior mass near δ = 0.

On the other hand, if we use grow, then for such very small δ ≠ 0 it is possible that we never reject, no matter how large our sample size, simply because it puts prior mass 0 in a neighbourhood around δ = 0; grow will only tend to reject at with power going to one if the actual δ is larger than the δ min plugged into the tuning parameter.
Superficially, it may seem that some frequentist methods can deal with arbitrarily small δ ≠ 0 without any additional tuning.
But in fact they need tuning just as much as our E-processes.
For example, the p < α test can be computed without the specification of a tuning parameter in the t-test setting -but only once we have decided on a sample size n.
text.formatted: For example, the p < α test can be computed without the specification of a tuning parameter in the t-test setting -but only once we have decided on a sample size n.

text.text: But to determine an n which will give us any reasonable power, we need an assumption on δ min after all; and worse, unlike for the mom, eGauss, and eCauchy E-processes, if our guess was too optimistic, we cannot continue sampling once we have exhausted our n initially planned points.

An alternative solution to taking a standard tuning parameter value such as g mom = 0.5 2 2 above, would be to run a pilot study, estimate the underlying effect size and use that as δ min in the designSaviT function.
On the other hand, if we are constrained by other quantities such as our budget for n plan , then insights can be gathered with the methods described in Section 2.5.

If we are interested in detecting arbitrarily small δ ≠ 0 in the prospective setting, and we have reached n plan without a rejection, we may accept the null for the time being, and hope that in the future we may obtain additional resources to allow us to continue collecting data.

On the other hand, if we do have a well-motivated choice for δ min , we may sometimes stop early because we can simultaneously reject all δ with |δ| ≥ δ min ; this would happen if all these larger δs fall outside an anytime-valid confidence interval, for instance, this happens in Fig. 10 for δ min = 1.5.

text.text: For this conclusion, we used data from a total of n1 = 1315 of n2 = 1324 participants, thus, on average n1 = 21.56 and n2 = 21.71 in each replication attempt.
In other words, this classical design required 2713 and 2650 fewer participants.
The one-sided e-value test allows for informed conclusions with even less data.
Tracking the e-value up to n plan = 37 or stopping as soon as e n ≥ 20 yields 51 times persuasive evidence for the effect, out of a total of 61 replication attempts (83.6%).
This evidence is gathered with a total of n1 = 1031 and n2 = 1062 participants, corresponding to an average of n1 = 16.90 and n2 = 17.41 per replication attempt.
Compared to the original set-up, stopping as soon as e n ≥ 1/α = 20 reduced the number of participants by 2997 in one group and 2912 in the other, resulting in roughly 73% resource savings.
This demonstration highlights the benefits of planned analyses in general, and efficiency of e-value based tests in particular.
The general conclusion remains the same if we tuned the E-process to the upper bound for δ min instead.
Hence, the precise specification of δ min is not necessary to gain efficiency and conserve resources.

If the magnitude of the data governing δ was indeed at least δ min , then we have provided such δ ample chance to yield persuasive evidence.
Since this did not occur for most replication attempts, we infer that the postulate δ ≥ δ min is unlikely with high probability.
Moreover, we come to this conclusion with 2012 and 2067 fewer participants per group, which is a reduction of 58.5% and 58.9% from the total sample sizes used in the original analysis.
We would like to reiterate the point that with e-values we do not have to stop at the first-passage time e n ≥ 1/α, nor at n plan .

Due to E-processes being robust to any stopping time, there is no need to discard newly available data once the test is conducted or the confidence interval is computed, as is the case with a classical analysis.

The fact that classical p < α tests and confidence intervals are only reliable when performed once -and only once -places undue pressure on well-intentioned researchers who seek to uphold the highest standards of research practice by pre-registering their confirmatory analyses.

text.text: Determining the appropriate sample size at which such a test or confidence interval should be computed is difficult.
This is especially true before experimentation has started when no data are present.
This problem is circumvented with e-value based methods, which can be used flexibly, allowing us to adapt the experiment to new information as they become available.
Only a few lines of code suffice, e.g.
R Code 2.1, to prospectively derive a power analysis with a non-binding planned sample size n plan based on an optimal (by default) mom type t-test E-process.

Analogous code can be used to construct optimal savi z-tests (i.e. designSaviZ), savi tests for two proportions (Turner, Ly, & Grünwald, 2024) (i.e. designSaviTwoProportions), savi logrank test (Ter Schure et al., 2024) (i.e. designSaviLogrank), and many more are scheduled to be implemented into the safestats R package (Ly, Turner, et al., 2026).

text.text: Ville's inequality guarantees that the probability of misleading evidence larger than 1/α remains bounded by α, despite flexible use of the optimised E-process.
Simulations under the alternative showed an increase in power compared to classical methods on average.
This increase in power translates into smaller expected sample sizes, which further highlights the non-binding nature of n plan .
The ability to derive more reliable conclusions with less data allows us to save time, money and effort that can be effectively allocated to other research endeavours.

For one set of replication attempts from the Many Labs 2 project, the use of an optimised E-process allows the number of participants to be reduced by more than 70% (Section 4.1), whereas it can result in a reduction of 58% in another set (Section 4.2).

These conclusions should not be viewed as criticism on the Many Labs 2 project, which did not exclusively focus on replicating a particular effect efficiently, but also aimed to examine the variation in replicability across samples and settings.
Once the data are collected, it is best to use them all, yielding narrower anytime-valid confidence intervals, thus, more precise inference of the effects of interest.

text.text: Unbiasedness is not promised by e-value methods, but they do promise to yield intervals that forever contain the true value with the advertised probability.
For large sample sizes, these intervals are guaranteed to yield unbiased estimates, as long as the interval widths shrink over time, as is the case for the mom type E-process.
The development of estimators that account for the bias due to using a specific data-dependent stopping time is still a subject of ongoing research.
The reciprocal of a Bayes factor is known to be interpretable as evidence in favour of the null against the alternative.
For instance, BF10 = 1/7 is interpreted as the data being seven times more likely under the null than under the alternative.

Despite its interpretability, this does not automatically imply that Ville's inequality holds in the other direction, not even if the Bayes factor is an E-process. 25 In other words, evidence as conveyed with an E-process not only requires interpretability, but also calibration in the frequentist sense (Chugg et al., 2026).

text.text: Nevertheless, as more and more data become available, the anytime-valid confidence interval provided by our E-process may get narrower and narrower around 0, and if this happens (as it does e.g. in Section 4.2 for the Macbeth effect), we may still informally conclude that 'to all practical intents and purposes, it seems the null is true' -just as is done in the context of classical frequentist confidence intervals.
When using e-value based inference, choices must be made regarding both the type of E-process to rely on (Section 3), and the tuning parameter within that type.

These choices thus introduce a level of subjectivity to the analysis, which might be viewed as undesirable: suppose a research group performs a psychological experiment and reports both the raw data and the corresponding evidence in terms of e-values; then a second group re-analyses the same data.
The second group gets a different result, if they use a different tuning parameter.
In simple settings, such as with t-tests, there is essentially only one reasonable p-value procedure, so both groups arrive at the same result.

While this may seem preferable, we should add that the classical t-test is not without a similarly subjective choice either: instead of choosing an E-process type and tuning parameter, we then have to choose the fixed sample size n at which the analyses will be performed based on a power analysis (van Zwet et al., 2023).
text.formatted: While this may seem preferable, we should add that the classical t-test is not without a similarly subjective choice either: instead of choosing an E-process type and tuning parameter, we then have to choose the fixed sample size n at which the analyses will be performed based on a power analysis <ref type="bibr" target="#b61">(van Zwet et al., 2023)</ref>.

text.text: Two different research groups doing both the experimental design and analysis will most likely get to quite a different sample sizes, and hence different results.
This subjective component becomes invisible when only one group gets to design the experiment, but it is there nevertheless.

It is also important to note that while the tuning parameter in the selection of the E-process takes the form of a prior distribution, the subjectivity it introduces differs fundamentally from that in Bayesian methods.

Specifically, the type I error guarantees of e-value based methods holds regardless of the choice of E-variable or prior: altering the prior affects only the statistical power, not the validity of the results.
Similarly, the choice of prior affects the width of an anytime-valid confidence interval, but it never compromises its validity.
By contrast, in Bayesian statistics, a badly informed prior leads to a bad posterior, and, subsequently, bad credible intervals see Grünwald (2023) and Appendix I and Fig. I² for further details.

text.text: Point 4 suggests that the methodology may be vulnerable to cherry-picking biases.
To ensure reliable inference with e-values, it is crucial to pre-register the chosen E-process, its tuning parameter, and the confirmatory hypotheses in advance.
What is not required, however, is strict adherence to a sampling plan, or even the specified significance thresholds.
We elaborate on this latter advantage below (cf. point ii) in the list of additional benefits of e-values.
The choice of priors can be viewed as an advantage, as it enables the integration of existing data to inform the design of E-processes.

Once chosen, the ensuing savi tests and anytime-valid confidence intervals will remain statistically sound, and the better the prior was informed, the narrower the confidence interval will tend to be (Grünwald, 2023).

text.text: iv.
Meta-Analysis Point 1 above shows how e-value-based methods might require more samples in the planning stage within a single study.
In contrast, the case for evalue methods is strongest in reproducibility studies such as Many Labs 2, where experiments are repeated many times.

Then the Law of Large Numbers kicks in and the average, rather than the worst-case, will determine what happens: Across studies, the e-value-based method almost certainly requires fewer data points than classical tests.
This principle also applies to meta-analyses, where e-values prove especially valuable (Grünwald, De Heide, & Koolen, 2024; Ter Schure et al., 2022).
text.formatted: This principle also applies to meta-analyses, where e-values prove especially valuable <ref type="bibr" target="#b15">(Grünwald, De Heide, & Koolen, 2024;</ref> <ref type="bibr">Ter Schure et al., 2022)</ref>.

text.text: In such settings, a meta-analytical e-value can be defined to robustly aggregate evidence as data accumulate across multiple studies.
The approach ensures type I error control, even when individual studies trigger replication attempts, differ in sample size, and are on-going.
The list above shows that e-values are far more than a tool for anytime-valid testing -they represent a new paradigm of inference, not just "yet another method".
Their key property is flexibility: they adapt not only to different sampling plans, but also enable the incorporation of prior knowledge and to data-dependent adjustments of significance thresholds.
This flexibility simplifies statistical practice.
By contrast, classical approaches impose rigid constraints that often obstruct, rather than advance scientific progress.
Reproducible and generalisable science certainly requires effort, but that effort should not be squandered on upholding outdated, rigid sampling plans that e-values render unnecessary.
In the present work we focussed on only null hypothesis testing problems.
Hence, data collection is stopped once the evidence against the null hypothesis, quantified by the e-value for significance when it crosses 1/α.
However, researchers are often also interested in testing whether the effect size is actually relevantly large.
If it is not, then we can also stop the experiment early and declare the effect uninteresting.
We already alluded to this possibility in Section 3.5, where we described an approach to do this based on anytimevalid confidence intervals.
However, the underlying E-processes are usually not optimised for this task.

A more suitable approach is to construct a specialised E-process against the hypothesis that the effect is relevantly large that is optimised to quickly gain evidence for the null, whenever the null holds true.
Data collection can then be stopped as soon as either the "standard" process exceeds 1/α or when the relevance process exceeds 1/α R .
The choice of suitable relevance processes is the subject of a forthcoming paper.
A further subject for future research is the development of savi tests for other standard testing problems in the social sciences.
There are currently savi versions available for the logrank test (Ter Schure et al., 2024), Fisher's exact test (Turner et al., 2024), Student's t-test, and linear regression (Lindon et al., 2026).

text.text: This procedure does not come with an n plan at which the detection of an effect |δ| ≥ δ min with at least, e.g. power = 80% is guaranteed.
Crucially, it also has an additional evidence boundary for accepting the null.
The latter is natural due to a Bayes factor less than 1 being interpreted as evidence for the null.
The current discussion in sequential Bayes factor testing revolves around (1) the selection of the boundaries A and B, thus, a specific stopping rule, and (2) which Bayes factor to use.
Type I and II errors are estimated based on simulations that depends on specific choice, most importantly, the chosen stopping rule.
For E-processes the stopping time is irrelevant, which makes its use easier and more straightforward.

To address the boundary question, Schönbrodt et al. (2017) suggested employing the eCauchy E-process/Bayes factor t-test, constructed with a Cauchy prior on δ s , featuring a prior width of 1, and decision boundaries set to A = 6 and B = 1/6 for early lines of research.

The Wald boundaries on their own, however, do not actually guarantee error control.
For instance, running Protocol 7.1 with boundaries A = 1-β α = 16, B = β 1-α = 0.21 and the computationally convenient Bayes factor of Eq.
(H4) leads to 16.8% correct null acceptance, but 24.9% false positive rejections, and no conclusion was reached for the remaining 58.2%.
The latter inconclusive category can lead to this procedure requiring more data points than the savi testing procedure.
Stopping rule dependent error control make the procedure less flexible.

For instance, during data acquisition a hopeful investigator changes his mind and continues sampling despite observing BF10 ≤ 0.21 by interpreting BF10 = 0.21 as only "moderate evidence" for the null (e.g. Jeffreys, 1961 , Appendix B, Lee & Wagenmakers, 2013).
text.formatted: For instance, during data acquisition a hopeful investigator changes his mind and continues sampling despite observing BF10 ≤ 0.21 by interpreting BF10 = 0.21 as only "moderate evidence" for the null (e.g. <ref type="bibr" target="#b22">Jeffreys, 1961</ref> <ref type="bibr">, Appendix B, Lee & Wagenmakers, 2013)</ref>.

text.text: Continuing sampling after hitting the lower boundary makes the sequential Bayes factor Protocol 7.1 equivalent to the savi testing Protocol 1.1 that has the potential to run indefinitely due to the absence of an n plan .
By Ville's inequality we know that halting as soon as BF10 ≥ 16 only guarantees a type I error of 6.25% under the null, if the Bayes factor is also an E-process.
If it is not, we cannot even say this, as is the case for the computationally convenient Bayes factor.

Assuming the Bayes factor is an E-process, a type I error guarantee of level α = 0.05 therefore forces the investigator to stop as soon as BF10 ≤ 0.21 so that the unaccounted probability of 1.25% can be absorbed by the lower boundary.
E-processes are robust to adaptation of the stopping rule, as it still defines a stopping time for which Ville's inequality holds.
This makes e-value based inference more flexible.
The additional stopping rule for the null also complicates the design of sequential Bayes factor tests.

To the best of our knowledge, all sequential Bayes factor tests require extensive simulations to provide an indication of both the realised type I and type II error, and they will all have to be re-performed when the stopping rule or the tuning parameter of the Bayes factor under consideration is changed.

In contrast, type I error control for Eprocesses is mathematically guaranteed by Ville's inequality, and type II error control and estimates of the run times of experiments can be obtained with much cheaper simulations.

Specifically, e-value sampling designs provide an indication of how long the experiment should run for in terms of n plan , and monitoring the test until n plan guarantees a 1 -β probability to detect effects |δ| ≥ δ min .
This n plan , in turn, is found by relatively quick simulations for typical values of α, β and δ min.

In this appendix we explore some subtleties concerning data dredging.
For concreteness, consider the following scenario: suppose a researcher initially followed Protocol 1.1, with α = 0.05 and n plan = 100.
His E-process never achieved 1/α = 20 before or at n plan .
Upon reaching sample size n plan , he stopped and noticed that the E-process achieved its maximum at, say, N = 37, when it obtained value e37 = 17.
After that, the e-values kept fluctuating; in particular, they reached a minimum of, say e95 = 2 and then increased again until e100 = 10.
The researcher may now be tempted to remove the consecutive block of outcomes X 38 , X 39 , . . . , X 94 from his sample.

Re-calculating the e-values on the modified data sequence X 1 , X 2 , . . . , X 37 , X 96 , . . . , X 100 , he finds that the final e-value is now 85, thus much larger than 1/α, so he can claim a rejection after all.

This is a serious form of data-dredging: the resulting output is not a valid e-value any more, and the probability, under the null, that, after removing 'the least favourable block of subsequent outcomes' from the data, the resulting 'e-value' is larger than 1/α, may very well be much larger than α -the type I error guarantee is violated.

Next, consider a milder form of data dredging: another researcher, confronted with the same data as above, might simply claim, a bit more modestly, that she stopped at N = 37, obtaining an e-value of e37 = 17.

This procedure of reporting the running maximum results in an invalid e-value, and thus amounts to cheating, for the simple reason that she determined N retroactively, after having observed more data.
Thus, she claims an output e N at a time N that is not a bona fide stopping time so it does not give us a valid E-variable.
While this reasoning is correct, there is a subtlety, since one might counter: doesn't Ville's inequality tell us that the probability, under the null, that E n will ever cross 1/α bounded by α?
So what harm can there be in reporting its maximum value observed so far?
After all, the type I error guarantee still holds!

While the observation that E n will, with high probability under the null, never cross 1/α is indeed correct (and in this sense the violation is less severe than the previous one), something can still go wrong.
To see why, consider the following follow-up scenario: after our researcher reported e37 = 17, the result was reported in a technical report and she turned her attention to other projects.

Yet, one year later, a new team of researchers, at a different lab, considers the same hypothesis test; they note that 'the threshold was almost achieved' and re-start data collection in as similar circumstances as possible, and keep updating their e-value, starting with the original researcher's 37 data points with e-value e37 = 17.

Then, effectively, they generate data points X 101 , X 102 , . . . and so on, and when, say, they cross the 1/α threshold after 15 new examples, what they have done really amounts to having thrown away all data points in-between X 37 and X 100 -and thus, they have ended up in the more serious form of data-dredging after all, which does break the type I error guarantee.

In other words, reporting the maximum e-value observed so far does preserve type I error guarantee if you have an absolute guarantee that the experiment forever be stopped, but it gets messed up under optional continuation.

More generally, as soon as the 'evidence' output by a researcher cannot be interpreted any more as the value of an E-process at a legitimate stopping time, there is a risk that, if data collection continuous, the type I error guarantee gets violated at some point in time.
